methodology: Loaded all 23 executable mock modules and applied the same Part 1/2 remap and Part 7 replacement used by the runtime boundary.

Read all 1,035 runtime-effective stimuli, instructions, passages, stems, options and keys; checked task-to-part correspondence, option counts, one-best-answer defensibility, accessibility for Saber 11 candidates and cross-mock consistency.
Verified every mock has exactly 45 questions, seven ordered parts and the declared 5/5/5/8/7/5/10 abbreviated distribution.
Compared the runtime-effective forms with current official ICFES descriptions, while treating the mocks as original practice and never as official, affiliated or psychometrically equivalent material.

Computed SHA-256 over each source file, the manifest content object, and a canonical JSON representation of each runtime-effective mock. Automated checks supported coverage and distribution analysis but did not substitute for semantic review.
Recorded uncertain one-best-answer cases as needs-adjudication and made no content, key, code, pricing or production changes.

checks.evidence: 23/23 runtime mocks contain 45 questions, Parts 1-7 in order, and counts 5/5/5/8/7/5/10.
After normalization the section styles are matching-grid, notices-grid, dialogs-grid, cloze-text, reading-text, reading-text and cloze-text for every mock.
No missing passage/stimulus required by style, duplicate normalized options, out-of-range keys, duplicate question IDs or non-sequential Part 4/7 blank labels were found.

All 23 manifest hashes describe raw modules, while runtime changes Parts 1/2 and replaces Part 7 through two shared files omitted from the reviewed candidate artifact set. All 23 runtime-effective hashes differ from manifest content hashes.
77/115 Part 2 items are not place-choice tasks; Parts 4 and 5 use four options rather than the current official three; Part 5 contains at least 35 stems requiring taxonomy adjudication.
Twenty-seven item-level cases need adjudication, mock-21 duplicates the Part 1 example word in the answer bank, and Part 7 exposes the same A/B/C/D/A/B/C/D/A/B key cycle in all 23 mocks.

The runner's abbreviated/non-official language is appropriate, but several public pages still call the ICFES offer 'simulacros completos'; a 45-item form with known format deviations cannot carry that unqualified claim.
This report is an independent board input and is not adjudication or final approval.

findings.proposedKeyOrWording: Make each runtime-effective mock hash a first-class candidate artifact and include normalize-icfes-mock.ts plus icfes-current-part-seven.ts in the candidate digest before accepting any content approval.
findings.evidence: The manifest contentHash covers each raw module, but normalizeIcfesMock swaps legacy Parts 1/2 and replaces all 230 Part 7 items from a shared file. Those shared dependencies are absent from the old candidate artifact set, and all 23 canonical runtime hashes differ from their manifest hashes.

findings.proposedKeyOrWording: Keep the visible label 'práctica propia abreviada · 45 preguntas' and never present these forms as reproducing the current 55-question standard form.
findings.evidence: Every internal mock correctly follows its declared 45-item 5/5/5/8/7/5/10 profile. The official 2026-2 guide describes a 55-item form with an 11/11/11/18/16/11/22 percent distribution, corresponding to 6/6/6/10/9/6/12 in the current product metadata.

findings.proposedKeyOrWording: Rewrite each affected stem and all three options so the student chooses the place where the notice could appear, or label the activity as supplemental pragmatic-notice practice rather than current-format Part 2.
findings.evidence: Only 38/115 runtime Part 2 items ask the student to choose a place. The remaining 77 ask directly about purpose, action, rule, audience or meaning; the current ICFES definition asks which place corresponds to the notice while using its communicative purpose as evidence.

findings.proposedKeyOrWording: Use three options A-C for each Part 4 blank, with distractors re-authored and independently adjudicated; otherwise label this as supplemental four-option cloze practice.
findings.evidence: All 184 Part 4 items and their instructions use four options A-D. The official 2026-2 Part 4 definition and example use three options A-C.

findings.proposedKeyOrWording: Use three options A-C for each Part 5 question and re-adjudicate distractor quality; otherwise label this as supplemental four-option reading practice.
findings.evidence: All 161 Part 5 items and their instructions use four options A-D. The official 2026-2 Part 5 definition and example use three options A-C.

findings.proposedKeyOrWording: Adjudicate each stem against the Part 5 literal-explicit/paraphrase construct; move genuinely inferential/global-evaluative items to Part 6 or rewrite them to target explicit information.
findings.evidence: At least 35 Part 5 stems explicitly request main idea/purpose/topic, suggestion, summary/tone/overall view, or phrase/word meaning. These are not automatically invalid, but they cross the declared boundary with Part 6 often enough that item-level classification is required before a current-format claim.

findings.proposedKeyOrWording: Reorder complete option texts with a deterministic, per-mock balanced plan, re-adjudicate every touched item, and bind the resulting runtime hashes.
findings.evidence: clozeQuestion sets answer=index%4. Consequently all 23 mocks repeat the identical ten-key cycle and all 230 items are predictable once a student sees the pattern.

findings.proposedKeyOrWording: Rebalance key positions within each mock and part without changing the keyed content, then rerun semantic review and hash binding.
findings.evidence: B or C holds 145/161 Part 5 keys (90.1%) and 100/115 Part 6 keys (87.0%). This cross-mock concentration creates a guessing cue and weakens assessment validity.

findings.proposedKeyOrWording: Use an example whose answer is distinct from all A-G words, or replace the duplicated A-G entry with a unique distractor while preserving five keyed words and two unused words.
findings.evidence: The runtime matching renderer appends exampleAnswer as an H entry. mock-21 already includes 'trophy' in the seven-word A-G bank, so the displayed bank has eight slots but only seven unique words and exposes a duplicate answer.

findings.proposedKeyOrWording: Normalize the ten question records to type='dialog' so metadata agrees with dialogs-grid and the other 21 mocks.
findings.evidence: These ten Part 3 questions are marked type='mcq'; all other runtime Part 3 items use type='dialog'. Rendering currently follows sectionStyle, so this is a metadata inconsistency rather than a visible task failure.

findings.proposedKeyOrWording: Make every catalog title match the executable mock title/theme, or explicitly explain that catalog labels are broad collections rather than the mock's topic.
findings.evidence: Twenty of 23 catalog titles disagree with the corresponding runtime title, for example mock-03 'Estudio y tecnología' vs 'Salud y cuerpo', mock-06 'Trabajo y carrera' vs 'Medio ambiente', and mock-08 'Ciencia y espacio' vs 'Familia y hogar'.

findings.currentKey: simulacros completos de ICFES; Simulacro completo
findings.proposedKeyOrWording: Use 'prácticas propias abreviadas para entrenar las siete partes' and retain the visible 45-vs-55 and non-affiliation disclaimer; reserve 'simulacro completo' for a form that matches the current standard and has passed the board.
findings.evidence: Unqualified complete-simulation claims remain in src/app/(site)/clases-de-ingles/page.tsx:49,617, src/app/(site)/clases-de-ingles-bucaramanga/page.tsx:239 and src/components/icfes/IcfesDashboardClient.tsx:64. The guided runner correctly says the 45-item practice does not reproduce the 55-item standard form.

findings.proposedKeyOrWording: Treat CEFR labels and score bands as orientation only unless a documented calibration study supports them; never describe the result as an official or predictive ICFES score.
findings.evidence: All mock files declare A2-B1 in comments, while the result layer reports estimated levels. This format review found no psychometric linking, standard setting or empirical difficulty evidence and therefore does not validate CEFR calibration or score equivalence.

findings.proposedKeyOrWording: Narrow the cooking method in the passage or replace 'fried' so only 'cooked' is defensible.
findings.evidence: In 'The dough is usually ___ on a griddle or pan over medium heat until golden', both 'cooked' and 'fried' can describe the process; the context does not exclude oil or frying.

findings.proposedKeyOrWording: Use a collocation that uniquely selects 'communication' or remove 'messages'.
findings.evidence: The sentence 'used only for voice ___' naturally allows both 'communication' and, in ordinary usage, 'messages'.

findings.proposedKeyOrWording: Rewrite the sentence to name social-network platforms or replace 'digital' and 'online' with incompatible distractors.
findings.evidence: 'Time people spend on ___ media' accepts 'social media', 'digital media' and 'online media' without additional context.

findings.proposedKeyOrWording: Use the conventional term 'natural regions' elsewhere in the sentence or replace 'zones'.
findings.evidence: 'The country is divided into several natural ___' allows both 'regions' and 'zones' on grammar and meaning alone.

findings.proposedKeyOrWording: Add context uniquely linking wet/dry periods to crops or replace tourism, industry and transport with nonparallel distractors.
findings.evidence: Wet and dry periods can directly affect agriculture, tourism, transport and parts of industry; the sentence provides no narrowing evidence.

findings.proposedKeyOrWording: Specify 'people who use' or replace accounts/members/followers with nonhuman/noncount distractors.
findings.evidence: 'Millions of active social media ___' accepts users and accounts, and can also describe members or followers depending on the measured population.

findings.proposedKeyOrWording: Name the object as an app/service or remove website and channel as viable alternatives.
findings.evidence: 'Access their favourite ___ to follow posts and stories' can reasonably refer to a platform, website or channel.

findings.proposedKeyOrWording: Add 'reshare with' or replace send/post with options incompatible with 'content with friends and family'.
findings.evidence: Users can share, send or post funny content with friends and family; the sentence does not force the keyed verb.

findings.proposedKeyOrWording: Provide a daily-frequency cue that excludes hour/week, or replace those time units.
findings.evidence: 'Some users visit several times a ___' is grammatical and plausible with hour, day or week.

findings.proposedKeyOrWording: Rewrite as 'a powerful marketing tool' or remove service/network/system as contextually plausible nouns.
findings.evidence: A social platform can be described as a powerful tool, network, system or service for small businesses.

findings.proposedKeyOrWording: Use 'city' directly in the passage or make distractors different entity types rather than alternative settlement labels.
findings.evidence: 'The ___ of Cartagena de Indias was founded ... in 1533' can grammatically and historically describe a city, town or settlement.

findings.proposedKeyOrWording: Use a uniquely selecting collocation or remove 'focus'.
findings.evidence: Memory can attract great attention or focus in research discourse; the passage does not decisively exclude focus.

findings.proposedKeyOrWording: Remove 'part' or rewrite around the unique collocation 'plays a critical role'.
findings.evidence: Both 'plays a critical role in memory formation' and 'plays a critical part in memory formation' are standard English.

findings.proposedKeyOrWording: Add 'possible for scientists' with a contrast that excludes ease, or replace 'easy'.
findings.evidence: Technology may make it possible or easy to observe processes in real time; the context does not state whether feasibility or effort is intended.

findings.proposedKeyOrWording: Add an explicit scheduling cue or remove 'energy'.
findings.evidence: Study advice can ask students to manage time or energy wisely; the next sentence supports time but does not make energy impossible.

findings.proposedKeyOrWording: Use 'taking notes' or replace 'lists'.
findings.evidence: 'Writing notes in class' is most conventional, but 'writing lists in class' remains grammatical and can involve putting information in one's own words.

findings.proposedKeyOrWording: Use 'short breaks' or replace walks/naps.
findings.evidence: 'Taking regular breaks/walks/naps allows your brain to rest' supports multiple options, even though breaks is the broadest.

findings.proposedKeyOrWording: Use 'review ... by rereading' with distractors that cannot express checking/repetition.
findings.evidence: 'Always ___ your key points by reading through your notes again' allows review, check and repeat in ordinary study advice.

findings.proposedKeyOrWording: Supply an uncertainty cue unique to 'might' or replace should/would.
findings.evidence: 'Choose a type you ___ enjoy' supports might, should and would under different ordinary meanings; no context establishes the intended modality.

findings.proposedKeyOrWording: Use 'when' as the key or revise the causal context so 'because' is uniquely justified.
findings.evidence: 'The painting was found ___ a family bought a house' naturally selects 'when'; the keyed 'because' asserts causation and is not the uniquely best temporal connector.

findings.proposedKeyOrWording: Add a determiner/quantity context that distinguishes 'other' from 'more', or replace 'more'.
findings.evidence: 'They found ___ beautiful paintings with this one' permits both other paintings and more paintings.

findings.proposedKeyOrWording: Keep either 'warning signs' or 'warning signals' and replace the other with a non-collocating distractor.
findings.evidence: 'Headache, dizziness and nausea can be early warning ___' has two standard completions: signs and signals.

findings.proposedKeyOrWording: Add speaker context that makes surprise the intended function, or replace the positive personal response.
findings.evidence: After 'I don't have any social media accounts', both the keyed surprise and 'You are very lucky then' are coherent natural replies.

findings.currentKey: B: Yes, it is considered some of the best quality.
findings.proposedKeyOrWording: Ask for agreement explicitly or replace the personal-preference response.
findings.evidence: 'I prefer to drink tea' is a natural conversational response to 'Colombian coffee is famous all over the world', even though the keyed agreement continues the proposition more directly.

findings.currentKey: B: That's one of the biggest and most vibrant festivals in Latin America.
findings.proposedKeyOrWording: Give the respondent an enthusiasm cue or replace the negative-opinion response.
findings.evidence: 'Carnivals are far too noisy for me' is a coherent reply to 'It's Carnival season in Barranquilla!', so personal stance rather than language competence separates it from the key.

findings.currentKey: C: That's a great deal — I'll try them on.
findings.proposedKeyOrWording: Add a prior affordability cue or replace the negative price judgment.
findings.evidence: 'Half price is still far too expensive' and the keyed positive purchase reaction are both natural replies to 'These jeans are on sale for half price.'

findings.currentKey: C: I'd love to sign up — it's a great way to help.
findings.proposedKeyOrWording: Add an invitation/interest cue or replace the refusal based on tiredness.
findings.evidence: 'I am too tired to go' is a coherent refusal to 'There is a community volunteering event this Saturday'; without context the key measures willingness, not a uniquely appropriate response.

limitations: This review evaluates format, task validity, instructions, one-best-answer defensibility, consistency and claim scope; it does not establish psychometric reliability, score comparability or CEFR calibration.
No similarity of structure or wording is treated as evidence of ICFES affiliation, authorization or official status.
This actor did not modify questions, answers, code, prices, manifests, deployment state or other reviewers' files and does not issue final board approval.
